title: Mood Indigo
composer: Duke Ellington, Barney Bigard and Irving Mills (Mitchell Parish lyrics claimed later)
personnel: Duke Ellington (piano, leader), Arthur Whetsel (trumpet), Joe "Tricky Sam" Nanton (trombone), Barney Bigard (clarinet), Fred Guy (banjo), Wellman Braud (bass), Sonny Greer (drums) and the rest of the Ellington orchestra
trivia: What made it famous is the odd trio voicing of muted trumpet, muted trombone and low-register clarinet. Ellington's band cut it for several labels within weeks in late 1930, and it became his signature slow number.

track.title: Mood Indigo
track.album: Mood Indigo (Victor 22587, 78 rpm single)
track.query: Duke Ellington and His Orchestra Mood Indigo 1930
track.notes: The Victor session of 10 Dec 1930; any of the early Dec 1930 / Oct 1930 Ellington originals is acceptable by artist and title, but not the later remakes (1940 Victor, 1950 Columbia, 1966 Reprise)

notes: DAHR gives the Victor session as 1930-12-10 (released about 23 Jan 1931). Ellington's first recording was the Brunswick of 1930-10-17, which is the version the Grammy Hall of Fame lists (Brunswick, 1930); the Victor is chosen as the best-known release. Personnel is the core band from Wikipedia plus the standard 1930 line-up (full sax/brass roster not re-verified). Duration approximate (not taken from a source).

trivia: Ellington's 1932 hit gave the name to a whole era; the title came from a phrase trumpeter Bubber Miley used. Ivie Anderson's vocal and Bigard's clarinet make this one of the first records to declare "swing" as a style before the swing era existed.

artist: Duke Ellington and His Famous Orchestra
title: Take the "A" Train
personnel: Duke Ellington (piano, leader), Wallace Jones, Rex Stewart, Ray Nance (trumpets), Joe Nanton, Lawrence Brown, Juan Tizol (trombones), Barney Bigard, Johnny Hodges, Otto Hardwick, Ben Webster, Harry Carney (reeds), Fred Guy (guitar), Jimmy Blanton (bass), Sonny Greer (drums)
trivia: Billy Strayhorn wrote it after Ellington gave him directions to Harlem, "take the A train". Ray Nance's muted trumpet solo is one of the most imitated in jazz, and the tune became the band's theme song.

title: I Can't Get Started
original_issue: Victor 36208 (12-inch 78 rpm, b/w The Prisoner's Song; Album C-28 "A Symposium of Swing")
personnel: Bunny Berigan (trumpet, vocal, leader), Joe Lipman (piano), George Wettling (drums) and the Berigan orchestra
trivia: Berigan sings the lyric and plays a long trumpet solo on this version, his lifelong signature piece. It was one of the most celebrated trumpet records of the swing era.

track.title: I Can't Get Started
track.album: A Symposium of Swing (Victor 36208, 12-inch)
track.query: Bunny Berigan and His Orchestra I Can't Get Started A Symposium of Swing 1937
track.notes: The 7 Aug 1937 Victor 12-inch recording (matrix CS-011675); not his 1936 Vocalion 10-inch version or later remakes

notes: DAHR: Victor matrix CS-011675, take 1, 8/7/1937, Victor 36208 released 9/1937, coupled with The Prisoner's Song. The Grammy list says Victor 1937; DAHR did not give the duration.

title: Georgia on My Mind
original_issue: Victor 23013 (78 rpm, b/w One Night in Havana)
personnel: Hoagy Carmichael (piano, vocal), Bix Beiderbecke (cornet), Jimmy Dorsey (clarinet, alto sax), Joe Venuti (violin), Eddie Lang (guitar) and other sidemen
trivia: Carmichael's first recording of his own song features Bix Beiderbecke's cornet on one of his last recording sessions, less than a year before he died. Ray Charles's 1960 version later made the song world-famous.

track.title: Georgia on My Mind
track.album: Georgia on My Mind / One Night in Havana (78 rpm single)
track.query: Hoagy Carmichael and His Orchestra Georgia on My Mind 1930
track.notes: Carmichael's 15 Sept 1930 Victor original; not Louis Armstrong's 1931 or Ray Charles's 1960 versions

notes: Date, label and B-side from the Wikipedia infobox. Victor catalog number, the personnel and the "one of Bix's last sessions" remark are from memory (Bix's presence is credited by the Grammy Hall of Fame); full sideman list not verified. Duration approximate (not taken from a source).

title: Stompin' at the Savoy
composer: Edgar Sampson, Benny Goodman and Chick Webb (lyrics Andy Razaf)
personnel: Chick Webb (drums, leader), Edgar Sampson (alto sax, arranger) and the Savoy Orchestra
trivia: Named after the Harlem ballroom where Webb's band ruled, the tune was composed by his saxophonist Edgar Sampson. Webb's recording was a hit in 1934, and Goodman made it a swing staple.

track.title: Stompin' at the Savoy
track.album: Stompin' at the Savoy (78 rpm single)
track.query: Chick Webb and His Orchestra Stompin' at the Savoy 1934
track.notes: The 18 May 1934 Chick Webb original; not Goodman's 1936 versions or the 1936 Trio/Quartet recordings

notes: Date, Columbia label and the 3:10 duration from the Wikipedia infobox; Columbia catalog number not found; sidemen not individually verified.

title: Tuxedo Junction
composer: Erskine Hawkins, Julian Dash and William Johnson (lyrics Buddy Feyne)
original_issue: Bluebird B-10409 (78 rpm, b/w Gin Mill Special)
personnel: Erskine Hawkins (trumpet, leader), Julian Dash (tenor sax) and the Hawkins orchestra
trivia: Named for a Birmingham, Alabama, streetcar junction that was the centre of the city's Black nightlife, the number was a big hit for Hawkins' band, and then even bigger for Glenn Miller.

track.title: Tuxedo Junction
track.album: Tuxedo Junction / Gin Mill Special (78 rpm single)
track.query: Erskine Hawkins and His Orchestra Tuxedo Junction 1939
track.notes: The 18 July 1939 Bluebird original; not the Glenn Miller, Andrews Sisters or Jan Savitt versions

notes: DAHR: Victor matrix BS-038421, 7/18/1939, Victor Studio 3, New York, Bluebird B-10409, released 9/11/1939, coupled with Gin Mill Special. Composer credits per DAHR (Hawkins, Dash, Johnson); lyricist from memory. Duration approximate (not taken from a source).

title: Boogie Woogie Bugle Boy
original_issue: Decca 3598 (78 rpm, b/w Bounce Me, Brother, with a Solid Four)
personnel: Patty, Maxene and LaVerne Andrews (vocals) with studio orchestra
trivia: A boogie-woogie novelty about a trumpeter drafted into the army, sung in tight three-part harmony. It became the Andrews Sisters' signature and one of the best-known songs of the war years.

track.title: Boogie Woogie Bugle Boy
track.album: Boogie Woogie Bugle Boy / Bounce Me Brother, with a Solid Four (78 rpm single)
track.query: The Andrews Sisters Boogie Woogie Bugle Boy 1941
track.notes: The 2 Jan 1941 Decca original, not the Bette Midler 1972 cover or the film versions

notes: DAHR: Decca 3598, DLA 2326 take B, 1/2/1941; the DAHR page does not name an arranger (Vic Schoen's role is from memory). Crossover: usually classed as pop/boogie-woogie vocal; kept as a swing-era vocal hit. Duration approximate (not taken from a source).

title: King Porter Stomp
personnel: Benny Goodman (clarinet, leader), Bunny Berigan (trumpet), Gene Krupa (drums), Harry Goodman (bass), Allan Reuss (guitar), Art Rollini (tenor sax) and the Goodman orchestra
trivia: Fletcher Henderson's arrangement of Jelly Roll Morton's tune, played by Goodman's band, made a dance-hall sensation of a decade-old New Orleans composition. Goodman's summer 1935 tour, climaxing at the Palomar in Los Angeles, is often taken as the birth of the swing era.

track.title: King Porter Stomp
track.album: King Porter Stomp / Sometimes I'm Happy (78 rpm single)
track.query: Benny Goodman and His Orchestra King Porter Stomp 1935
track.notes: The 1 July 1935 Victor studio recording with the Henderson arrangement; not Jelly Roll Morton's own versions or the 1938 Carnegie Hall performance

notes: Date, Victor number and the release date of 31 July 1935 from oldtimeblues.net and Wikipedia; the personnel listing there includes Berigan, Krupa, Allan Reuss, Harry Goodman and Art Rollini but I did not verify the full roster. Coupling from memory. Duration approximate (not taken from a source).

title: (Hep-Hep!) The Jumpin' Jive
composer: Cab Calloway, Frank Froeba and Jack Palmer
personnel: Cab Calloway (vocal, leader), Mario Bauzá (trumpet), Chu Berry (tenor sax) and the Calloway orchestra
trivia: A jive-talk dance number recorded for Vocalion in 1939 with Chu Berry's tenor in the band. The song is still a favourite with swing revival bands, and the Grammy Hall of Fame inducted it in 2017.

track.title: (Hep-Hep!) The Jumpin' Jive
track.album: (Hep-Hep!) The Jumpin' Jive (Vocalion single)
track.query: Cab Calloway and His Orchestra (Hep-Hep!) The Jumpin' Jive 1939
track.notes: The 17 July 1939 Calloway/Vocalion original; not the Lionel Hampton (June 1939) or later swing-revival versions

notes: Date (17 July 1939) from Wikipedia and a fan wiki; Vocalion catalog number not found; Dizzy Gillespie did not join until later, so he is not listed. A DAHR search surfaced Lionel Hampton's separate June 1939 Victor version, which is not the card recording. Duration approximate (not taken from a source).

artist: Gene Krupa and His Orchestra (vocal Anita O'Day, trumpet Roy Eldridge)
title: Let Me Off Uptown
personnel: Gene Krupa (drums, leader), Anita O'Day (vocal), Roy Eldridge (trumpet) and orchestra
trivia: Anita O'Day's cheeky invitation to Roy Eldridge to "blow" was the band's biggest hit of 1941. The trumpet-and-vocal banter made O'Day's name and added to Eldridge's fame.

track.title: Let Me Off Uptown
track.album: Let Me Off Uptown / Flamingo (78 rpm single)
track.query: Gene Krupa and His Orchestra Let Me Off Uptown 1941
track.notes: The May 1941 OKeh studio recording with O'Day and Eldridge; not the 1956 remake

notes: Wikipedia gives recording as May 1941 (exact day not found), release June 1941; coupling per Wikipedia infobox. Radio Swiss Jazz lists a 1956 recording which is a separate remake. The OKeh catalog number was not found. Duration approximate (not taken from a source).

title: Moten Swing
composer: Bennie and Buster Moten (Eddie Durham arrangement; authorship disputed)
personnel: Bennie Moten (leader), Count Basie (piano), Hot Lips Page (trumpet), Eddie Durham (trombone, guitar, arranger), Ben Webster, Eddie Barefield (reeds), Walter Page (bass)
trivia: Moten's Kansas City band, which included Basie and several future stars, cut this riff-based number in Camden, New Jersey. After Moten died in 1935, Basie took over the band's style and sound.

track.title: Moten Swing
track.album: Moten's Swing (Victor 23384, 78 rpm single)
track.query: Bennie Moten's Kansas City Orchestra Moten Swing Moten's Swing 1932
track.notes: The 13 Dec 1932 Victor recording; not the later Basie versions

notes: DAHR: Victor matrix BS-74847, 12/13/1932, Camden NJ, Victor 23384 (not 23038). Release year 1933 is an estimate; personnel from memory/Wikipedia, not re-verified (DAHR lists the instrumentation only). Duration approximate (not taken from a source).
